chapter_theme: The second half of the Vaazhthu Kaathai is a cycle of women's play songs that divides the praise among the three crowns: the ammanai songs sing the Chola's ancestral deeds and Puhar, the ball songs hail the Pandya whom Kannaki has just declared blameless, the swing songs sing the Chera line's deeds, the pounding songs give each city its women and its king, and the close has Kannaki herself praise Senguttuvan; no karma is named in this half.

cast.role: the women of Vanchi who play the ammanai, ball, swing and pounding songs of the Vaazhthu Kaathai
Kovalan's wife, the pathini who burned Madurai, now a goddess
the Chera king of Vanchi who brought the stone from the Himalaya for Kannaki's image

silappathikaram:29:105-107.reading: The last stanza of the benediction calls the company to sing, and sing again, the lord of the Kaveri country and Puhar of the flower-strewn tresses.
silappathikaram:29:105-107.nuance: The Pandya and Chera stanzas before it (97-100, 101-104) each praise a deed of the king and close with வாழியரோ and the king's old line; this Chola stanza has no deed and no வாழியரோ, only the call to sing, so it is either a shorter form or a broken one. The Chola is named only by his country, and the line gives Puhar the woman's epithet பூவிரி கூந்தல், as if the city were a woman.

silappathikaram:29:108-112.reading: The first ammanai song asks, as the women toss their play-stones, who ruled the sea-fenced world and guarded the high fortress of the king of the gods, answers that it was the Chola who destroyed the three hanging forts in the sky, and bids them sing his city Puhar.
silappathikaram:29:108-112.nuance: The ammanai form is a riddle and its answer: one line asks யார் அம்மானை, the next repeats the clue and answers with காண் அம்மானை, and the refrain turns from the king to his city. So the two deeds, guarding Indra's fort and cutting down the hanging forts, are set as one king's, and the song names no Chola king by his own name.

silappathikaram:29:113-117.reading: The second ammanai song asks who was the king who, while heaven praised him, entered the scale for a dove and cut his own flawless body, answers that he was the guardian who gave justice to the milch cow that came before him, and bids them sing his flowering Puhar.
silappathikaram:29:113-117.nuance: The riddle's form makes the body-cutting king and the king who judged for the cow one answer, where Kannaki's plea at the Pandya's court (20:55-73) gave them as two Chola precedents; whether the song means one man or one line is not settled by the Tamil. The deeds Kannaki used to accuse a Pandya are sung here, in the Chera capital, as the plain glory of Puhar.

silappathikaram:29:118-122.reading: The third ammanai song asks who stamped his sword-bright tiger on the northern mountain while the eight mountains of the quarters looked on without blinking, answers that it was the victor who took the eight directions under the shade of his umbrella and protected them, and bids them sing his Puhar.
silappathikaram:29:118-122.nuance: The song does not name the king; the tiger on the Himalaya is the deed the Puhar book gives to Thirumavalavan (5:89-110), where the mountain halts him. Here the eight guardian mountains only watch, and the halt has become a rule over all eight quarters.

silappathikaram:29:123-128.reading: The fourth ammanai song, of the women themselves, asks what is the worth of the singing the jewelled women do in their homes with the ammanai in their hands, answers that it is that the garlanded king should come to their round, painted breasts, and says that if the king of the line comes there, they will sing his lovely Puhar.
silappathikaram:29:123-128.nuance: The game turns from the king's deeds to the singers' desire for him: the play-song is offered as a lure for his embrace. The king is again only தார்வேந்தன், குலவேந்தன், not named, and the refrain still ends on Puhar.

silappathikaram:29:129-132.reading: The first ball song shows a girl like a golden creeper, her gold garland flashing and her girdle-bells ringing, running everywhere and striking the ball while she cries long live the Southerner, long live the one whose chest bears the gods' necklace.
silappathikaram:29:129-132.nuance: The ball songs praise the Pandya alone (தென்னன், and தேவர் ஆர மார்பன், the king who wore the necklace of the king of the gods): sung in the Chera city after the Pandya's death, they follow Kannaki's word just before (78-83) that the Pandya is blameless and is now Indra's guest.
silappathikaram:29:129-132.event: The girls play at ball, crying blessings on the Pandya with each stroke.

silappathikaram:29:133-136.reading: The second ball song likens the player, darting back and forth on every side, rising and turning, to a young creeper of lightning come down to the wide earth, as she strikes the ball with the same cries for the Pandya.
silappathikaram:29:133-136.event: A girl runs and leaps after the ball, crying blessings on the Pandya.

silappathikaram:29:137-140.reading: The third ball song says the ball, coming close, never rested in the hand and, rising from the long earth, never reached the heights, and closes with the same cries for the Pandya as it is struck.
silappathikaram:29:137-140.nuance: Lines 137-138 seem to describe the ball kept always between hand and sky, never caught and never lost upward; மந்தரம் may be the sky or Mount Mandara, and the sense is not sure.
silappathikaram:29:137-140.event: The girls keep the ball in the air, crying blessings on the Pandya.

silappathikaram:29:141-145.reading: The first swing song bids the girls seat Aiyai on the jewelled swing hung on ropes, push it together with lifted hands, and swing with long eyes darting, singing the guardian who cut the kadamba down at its root and the emblem of the curved bow.
silappathikaram:29:141-145.nuance: The swing songs belong to the Chera. கடம்பு முதல் தடிந்த is the Patitruppattu's own phrase for Neduncheralathan's deed (patitruppattu:20), but the song names no king, so the deed is sung as the Chera line's glory before Senguttuvan. ஐயை may be Madari's daughter, whom Devanthi has just pointed out among the heavenly company (72), or a word for a lady; the singers' own swing would make the second reading possible.
silappathikaram:29:141-145.event: The girls set a companion on the swing and push it as they sing.

silappathikaram:29:146-150.reading: The second swing song sings the might of the Chera, Poraiyan, Malaiyan, who without stint fed the great feast to the war in which the Five and the twice fifty rose against each other, and bids them swing with dark hair flying, singing his cutting of the kadamba.
silappathikaram:29:146-150.nuance: The feast at the war of the five and the hundred is the deed Purananuru 2 gives by name to Uthiyan Cheralathan; the song gives it to the Chera by his house names (சேரன், பொறையன், மலையன்) and sets it beside the kadamba deed of another king, so it praises the line, not one man.

silappathikaram:29:151-155.reading: The third swing song sings the might of the king who guards all living people, the lord of the bow who, it seems, holds the fish and the tiger, and who ruled from the rich land of the harsh-tongued Yavanas and the great mountain to Kumari in the south, and bids them swing with slender waists swaying, singing the emblem of the victorious bow.
silappathikaram:29:151-155.nuance: செருவிற் கயற்புலியான் can be read as the king of the battle-bow who also bears (or has taken) the Pandya's fish and the Chola's tiger; if so, the Chera song folds all three crowns' emblems into its own king, where the Madurai kuravai (17:1-10) set the three side by side on the Himalaya. The reading of the compound is not certain.

silappathikaram:29:156-160.reading: The first pounding song says the women of Puhar, in the shade of flowering kaanchi, pound rich pearls with sweet sugarcane for pestles, and that the song to sing is the one of the Chembiyan of the strong chariot with the wheel banner and the shoulders like great hills, the one the girls cry out.
silappathikaram:29:156-160.nuance: Each of the three pounding songs gives one city its women, its pestle and its king: the luxury is formal (pearls in place of grain, cane or coral or ivory in place of a pestle), and the work song is turned to praise. The order here is Chola, Pandya, Chera, ending on the host.

silappathikaram:29:161-165.reading: The second pounding song says the women of towered Madurai pound pearls worthy of song with coral pestles, and that the song to sing is of the fish banner of the Panchavan, whose shoulders shine with the necklace of the king of the gods, the song that sinks into the heart of the neem-garlanded king.
silappathikaram:29:161-165.nuance: The last line, the song that 'melts' or 'enters' the heart of the neem-garlanded one (வேப்பந்தார் நெஞ்சுணக்கும்), lets the song reach the Pandya himself, now in Indra's world by Kannaki's word.

silappathikaram:29:166-170.reading: The third pounding song says the women of Vanchi pound fine pearls in a sandalwood mortar with ivory pestles, and that the song to sing is the one that spread over the land and covered it, the report of the Chera of the conquering garland who cut down the kadamba, the song that wins the palmyra-wearer's heart.

silappathikaram:29:171-174.reading: The close says that the kings of the long earth who do not bow at the good feet of Poraiyan of the long bow find it hard to live, and that, her vow fulfilled, our king's lady too praised him: long live Senguttuvan for ages.
silappathikaram:29:171-174.nuance: எங்கோ மடந்தை takes up the Vanchi women's claim earlier in the kaathai (93) that Kannaki is the Chera's daughter, against the Madurai women's claim that she is the Pandya's; so the close ends with the goddess on the Chera's side. சூளொழிய may mean that her vow (to destroy Madurai) is now spent, or 'without an oath'; and வாழ்த்தல் in line 172 may be a slip for வாழ்தல், which the reading follows. This is the only unit in the song cycle that names a living king.
silappathikaram:29:171-174.event: Kannaki, now a goddess, joins in praising Senguttuvan.

claims.claim: kings who will not bow to the Chera's feet cannot long prosper

links.note: The Puram poem tells Killivalavan that giving, conquest and justice are not his own fame, since his line already holds the king who entered the scale for the dove and the ancestors who destroyed the hanging fort; the ammanai answers its riddle with the Chola who destroyed the hanging forts and names no living Chola.
links.teaches: Read together, the Puram poet's warning that the ancestors' deeds swallow a living Chola's fame comes true in the epic, where Chola praise sung at the Chera court consists of nothing but those ancestral deeds and the city of Puhar.

gains.a: the riddle's answer gains its old standing: the hanging fort was already the Chola line's inherited title in the Sangam praise of a named king
gains.b: the Puram poem's claim that ancestral glory outshines the present king gains a later case in which the line is remembered only by it, in a rival kingdom's women's game

links.note: Kannaki before the Pandya recalls the Chola who relieved a bird's distress and the one who crushed his son under the wheel for a cow, to accuse a king who did not inquire; the ammanai sings the dove-king and the cow's justice as the glory of Puhar, after Kannaki has declared the Pandya blameless.
links.teaches: The same two Chola precedents change use across the story: in Madurai they are Kannaki's weapon against a Pandya, and in Vanchi, once she has cleared him, they are a girls' refrain beside ball songs hailing that same Pandya, so the standard of justice survives the verdict while losing its edge.

links.note: The Puhar book tells how Thirumavalavan went north, was stopped by the Himalaya and carved his tiger on it; the ammanai sings a king who stamped his tiger on the northern mountain while the eight mountains of the quarters watched, and ruled all eight directions under his umbrella.
links.teaches: Set beside the narrative, the song shows the epic's praise turning a halt into a triumph: the mountain that ended Valavan's march becomes a witness, and one carving on one peak becomes rule of the eight quarters.

links.note: Kannaki, appearing in the sky to Senguttuvan, says the Southerner is blameless and has become a guest in the palace of the king of the gods, and that she is his daughter; the ball songs that follow hail the Southerner with the gods' necklace at every stroke.
links.teaches: The ball songs are the public form of Kannaki's acquittal: only because she has called the Pandya blameless can the women of the Chera city hail the king who killed her husband, and his old title of the gods' necklace now reads as his place in Indra's hall.

links.note: The Patitruppattu poem names Neduncheralathan as the king who went against his foes on an island in the sea and cut down the kadamba at its root (கடம்புமுதல் தடிந்த); the swing song sings the guardian who cut the kadamba at its root (கடம்பு முதல் தடிந்த) and the emblem of the bow, and names no king.
links.teaches: The pair shows the Patitruppattu's title for one Chera king passing into the epic as an unnamed dynastic refrain, so that in Senguttuvan's court a deed the Sangam decade credits to Neduncheralathan is sung as the house's own.

gains.a: the swing song's unnamed guardian gains an identity: the phrase is the title of Neduncheralathan in the Chera court poetry
gains.b: the Patitruppattu's title gains evidence of its afterlife, as a stock phrase of the Chera line sung by women at play rather than a bard's praise of one patron

links.note: Murinjiyur Mudinagarayar praises Uthiyan Cheralathan as the one who gave the great feast without limit while the Five and the hundred fought until the hundred fell; the swing song gives the feast at the war of the Five and the twice fifty to the Chera, Poraiyan, Malaiyan, by house names only, and pairs it with the kadamba deed.
links.teaches: The Puram poem binds the feast to one named king, while the epic gives it to the Chera house in general and sets it beside another king's deed, so the pair shows a single patron's distinction becoming an heirloom any Chera can be sung by.

gains.a: the swing song's line gains its source and the king it belonged to, Uthiyan Cheralathan, whom it does not name
gains.b: the Puram poem's claim gains a measure of its fame: generations later it is still the Chera line's mark, though detached from the king it praised

links.note: The Madurai herdswomen's book opens on the Pandya whose fish is written on the brow of the Himalaya with the tiger and the bow written beside it; the Vanchi swing song sings the king of the bow who holds the fish and the tiger and rules from the Yavana land to Kumari.
links.teaches: The two songs claim the same three emblems for different kings: Madurai sets the Pandya's fish first with the Chola and Chera signs beside it, and Vanchi folds fish and tiger into the Chera's bow, so the epic's praise of the three crowns is a set of rival boasts that its songs leave standing side by side.

links.note: The couplet asks what learning is worth to those who do not bow at the good feet (நற்றாள் தொழாஅர்) of the one of pure knowledge; the close says kings who do not bow at the good feet (நல் தாள் தொழார்) of Poraiyan find it hard to live, and Kannaki too praises Senguttuvan.
links.teaches: The close moves the Kural's phrase for bowing to the god's feet onto a living Chera king and makes the penalty for not bowing the loss of life rather than of learning's fruit, while the deified Kannaki joins the praise, so the epic ends by turning a devotional formula into a political one.

gains.a: the closing boast gains the weight of the formula it borrows: bowing at the good feet is the Kural's posture before the god
gains.b: the couplet's phrase gains a case of its wording transferred from the god to a king, which shows how its language of worship could be turned to royal praise

source_issues: Lines 105-107, the Chola stanza of the benediction, have three lines where the Pandya and Chera stanzas (97-100, 101-104) have four, no deed and no வாழியரோ refrain, and line 105 (எல்லா நாம்) is a half line; the stanza may be a different form or a damaged one.
The edition prints song number 21 after song 28 at line 174; read as 29 (show flags it).
Line 172 reads வாழ்த்தல் where the sense ('find it hard to live') wants வாழ்தல்; possibly a misprint.
Line 137 ends நீணிலம் and line 138 begins தன்னினின்று, so the line division runs across the phrase; the sense of 137-138 is not secure.
